subject: Basic Mathematics
introduction: Combinatorics counts arrangements and selections. Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections. Probability = favorable outcomes / total outcomes. Mastering when to multiply (AND) vs add (OR) probabilities is essential.

key_formulas.name: Stars and Bars
key_formulas.formula: C(n+k-1, k-1) \text{ ways to put n identical items into k bins}

tips_and_tricks: Permutation: ORDER matters (passwords, rankings). Combination: order doesn't matter (committees, groups).
Circular arrangements: (n-1)! ways (fix one item, arrange the rest).
C(n,r) = C(n, n-r). Use whichever is easier.
Multiply probabilities for AND (sequential events). Add for OR (mutually exclusive).

worked_examples.title: Example 1: Committee selection
worked_examples.question: A committee of 5 must be chosen from 4 men and 6 women, with at least 2 men. How many ways?

worked_examples.title: Example 2: Probability of drawing cards
worked_examples.question: From a deck of 52, draw 2 without replacement. P(both are aces)?
solution: Step 2: P(2nd is ace | 1st was ace) = 3/51 = 1/17.

questions.subject: Basic Mathematics
questions.question_text: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using {0,1,2,3,4,5} without repetition and divisible by 5?
questions.explanation:
Divisible by 5: last digit is 0 or 5.

Case last=0: First digit: 5 choices (1-5), then 4 remaining for 2 middle: 5×4 = 20. Total: 1×5×4×1=20.
Case last=5: First digit: 4 choices (1-4), middle: from remaining 4 digits: 4×3=12. Total: 4×4×3×1=48... 

Wait: Case 0: _ _ _ 0. First: any non-zero from {1,2,3,4,5}=5; 2nd: 4; 3rd: 3. → 5×4×3=60.
Case 5: _ _ _ 5. First: {1,2,3,4}=4; 2nd: from remaining 4; 3rd: 3 → 4×4×3=48.
Total=60+48=108... 

Let me recalculate systematically. Digit set {0,1,2,3,4,5}. 4-digit: first ≠ 0.
Last=0: P(5,3)=60 (first 3 from {1,2,3,4,5})
Last=5: first from {1,2,3,4}=4 choices, next 2 from remaining 4: 4×3=12. So 4×12=48.
Total=108. None match! Reconsidering: if set is {1,2,3,4,5,6} or if repetition allowed...
hints: Number divisible by 5: last digit is 0 or 5.
Case last=0: first 3 positions from {1,2,3,4,5} = P(5,3)=60.
Case last=5: first ≠ 0, from {1,2,3,4}, rest from remaining. Add both cases.

questions.subject: Basic Mathematics
questions.question_text: 6 people in a line. 3 specific people must not all be adjacent. How many arrangements?
questions.explanation:
Total = 6! = 720
A,B,C all adjacent: treat as block → 4!×3! = 24×6 = 144

Valid = 720-144 = **576**

*Exact answer depends on interpretation. 576 is standard.*
hints: Treat 3 specific people as one block: 4! arrangements × 3! internal = 144.

questions.subject: Basic Mathematics
questions.question_text: Distribute 8 identical candies into 3 distinct boxes with none empty. How many ways?
questions.explanation:
**Stars and bars (none empty):**

Subtract 1 from each box: 8-3 = 5 candies to distribute freely.
C(5+3-1, 3-1) = C(7,2) = **21**
hints: None empty: subtract 1 from each box first. New problem: distribute 8-3=5 freely.
Stars and bars: C(n+k-1, k-1) = C(7,2).
